meta.case_name: High Engineer Attrition at SLS Oil Gas Services

prompt.context: Our client SLS is one of the world's largest oil and gas services provider operating in 85 countries and employing about 100,000 people from over 140 countries. They help find, scope and drill as much oil and gas as possible for their clients – which range from major international oil companies to petrostates such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Of late they are seeing a very high attrition rate among their Field Engineer (FE) population across several offices globally, the Mumbai office in India being one of the most affected. The CEO is concerned and has asked you for advice specifically for the Mumbai office. She hopes that if the problem can be fixed in Mumbai, similar fix can be implemented everywhere else. It is indeed a matter of grave urgency for SLS.
prompt.question: Identify the cause(s) of high attrition among Field Engineers in SLS's Mumbai office and make recommendations on how to fix it.

clarifying_info.q: What does a Field Engineer do?
clarifying_info.a: Field Engineers work with specialized oilfield equipment which they lower inside a well, and then record and analyze data to identify whether and how much oil and gas is buried in the ground. They spend a considerable amount of time working on oil rigs. All oil rigs in Mumbai are offshore i.e. at sea. Most offshore rigs are bad with poor food, poor internet and poor accommodation.
(No. of FEs quitting in a year / Avg. no. of FEs in that year) %

clarifying_info.q: Where are FEs going when they leave?
clarifying_info.a: Mostly going to do Masters or moving to a completely different industry.

clarifying_info.q: How high is the attrition rate?
clarifying_info.a: 28% in 2016 in Mumbai (similarly high in several other offices globally).

clarifying_info.q: What has the CEO specifically requested?
clarifying_info.a: Identify the cause(s) of high attrition and make recommendations on fixing it.

exhibits.title: Types of Offshore Oil Rigs in Mumbai
exhibits.shows: Two types of offshore oil rigs used in Mumbai operations: a Semi-submersible (semi-sub) and a Deepwater drillship.

exhibits.title: Mumbai FE Headcount and Attrition Data (2012–2016)
exhibits.shows: A table of annual FE headcount data for the Mumbai office from 2012 to 2016, tracking engineers at start/end of year, hires, firings, quits, transfers in, transfers out, and computed attrition percentage.
exhibits.data: 2012: start 50, end 52, hired 6, fired 1, quit 2, transferred out 4, transferred in 3, attrition 3.9%; 2013: start 52, end 55, hired 6, fired 2, quit 3, transferred out 3, transferred in 5, attrition 5.6%; 2014: start 55, end 51, hired 5, fired 1, quit 7, transferred out 1, transferred in 0, attrition 13.2%; 2015: start 51, end 50, hired 2, fired 0, quit 10, transferred out 0, transferred in 7, attrition 19.8%; 2016: start 50, end 50, hired 6, fired 0, quit 14, transferred out 0, transferred in 8, attrition 28.0%

exhibits.title: Utilization & Effective Utilization Trends (2012–2016)
exhibits.shows: A line chart with two series — Utilization (% of FEs not on vacation) and Effective Utilization (% of FEs offshore) — from 2012 to 2016. The gap between the two lines widens over time.
exhibits.data: Both series shown from 2012 to 2016; Utilization runs higher (~80%) and Effective Utilization runs lower (~60%) in recent years with the gap visibly widening

exhibits.title: Level Loading – FE Time Offshore (Single Stretch)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the distribution of the FE population by how long they spend offshore in a single stretch, with buckets: <1 week, 1–2 weeks, 2–3 weeks, 3–4 weeks, >4 weeks.
exhibits.data: Bars for <1 week, 1–2 weeks, 2–3 weeks, 3–4 weeks, >4 weeks; optimal offshore stretch known to be ~3 weeks

exhibits.title: Level Loading by Seniority (Sr. vs Jr. FEs)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart segmenting the level-loading distribution from Exhibit 4 by seniority — Senior FEs and Junior FEs — to reveal whether the distribution of offshore stretch lengths differs between the two groups.
exhibits.data: Two series (Sr. and Jr.) across buckets <1 week, 1–2 weeks, 2–3 weeks, 3–4 weeks, >4 weeks; Sr. FEs skew toward longer stretches (>4 weeks) and Jr. FEs skew toward shorter stretches (<2 weeks)

framework: 1. Understand the business context in Mumbai and the life of an FE: (a) what SLS does in Mumbai; (b) FE background, day-in-the-life, work-life balance, relationship with managers

2. Identify reasons for high attrition: (a) how to collect information (interviews with FEs first, then managers/HR; anonymous questionnaires); (b) analyze potential reasons — internal (SLS-related) vs. external (non-SLS-related)
3. Develop recommendations: (a) short-term fixes; (b) long-term structural changes

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 2. What key observations do you draw from the Mumbai FE headcount data?
questions.guidance: Strong answers note: (1) total FE count is roughly constant at ~50 despite 25 rigs and steady activity over 5 years; (2) number of FEs quitting has risen dramatically from 2 (2012) to 14 (2016); (3) transfers out dropped to 0 from 2015 — a management decision that may be demotivating; (4) transfers in have been rising (7–8 in 2015–2016) — influx of new recruits may be harming team cohesion.

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 3. What does the widening gap between Utilization and Effective Utilization tell you?
questions.guidance: Utilization (% not on vacation) has risen while Effective Utilization (% offshore) has fallen — meaning more FEs are sitting in the office rather than being offshore or on vacation. Since bonuses are earned offshore, FEs are missing bonus while also missing vacation time. This signals a management issue: the new risk-averse management (post-2014) is keeping more FEs on reserve in the office instead of sending them offshore or on vacation.

questions.prompt: Math question (a): Based on Exhibits 2 & 3, calculate the number of FEs expected to be in the office on any given day.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the 2016 figures: 50 FEs total, Utilization ~80%, Effective Utilization ~60%. Calculate FEs at work, FEs offshore, FEs in office, and FEs on vacation.

steps: FEs in office (at work but not offshore) = 40 − 30 = 10
math.answer: 10 FEs are in the office on any given day; 10 are on vacation.

questions.prompt: Math question (b): Given only 2 FEs are needed in the office, 1 standby FE per rig for 25 rigs, and 36% of rigs have active operations (requiring a 2nd FE sent offshore), how high can effective utilization be taken and how many FEs can be sent on vacation?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recall the staffing model: 1 standby FE per rig plus 1 additional FE sent during operations. Calculate total FEs needed offshore, derive the maximum effective utilization, then determine how many FEs can go on vacation.

math.setup: 25 rigs; 1 standby FE per rig; 36% of rigs have operations requiring a 2nd FE; only 2 FEs needed in the base office; total FEs = 50
steps: FEs that can go on vacation = 50 − 34 − 2 = 14
math.answer: Effective utilization can be raised to 68%; 14 FEs can be sent on vacation.

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 4. What does the level loading chart show, and what follow-up would you ask?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 4 shows the distribution of FEs by how long they stay offshore in a single stretch. Optimal is ~3 weeks. A strong candidate notices a wide spread — some FEs spending very short stretches and others very long — and asks to segment this data by seniority (leading to Exhibit 5).

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 5. What does the level loading vs seniority chart reveal, and what explains it?
questions.guidance: Senior FEs are spending disproportionately long stretches offshore (>4 weeks), while Junior FEs are spending short stretches (<2 weeks) and therefore earning less bonus. Both groups are unhappy for opposite reasons. The root cause: the new risk-averse management (post-2014) lacks confidence in Junior FEs' competency and therefore relies on Senior FEs for operations, overloading them while underutilizing Juniors.

questions.prompt: What are the key internal and external reasons for high attrition, and how would you collect this information?
questions.guidance: Collection approach: interview FEs first (before managers/HR), in person preferred over questionnaires, asking about managers, motivation, peer exit reasons, and whether SLS meets their expectations. Internal reasons: management change in 2014 (risk-averse, keeping more FEs on reserve); fewer vacations and more office time without bonus; long offshore runs for Sr. FEs; no transfer-outs (FEs stuck in same office for years); large influx of new recruits reducing team cohesion. External reasons: FEs going for Masters or switching industries — wrong recruiting targets; compensation gap vs. comparable companies narrowing; booming startup culture in India with growing exit options.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific recommendations would you make to fix attrition — both short-term and long-term?

categories.name: Short-term
ideas: Train management — make the offshore staffing system process-driven rather than people-driven
Increase vacation/time-off by reducing utilization while increasing effective utilization
Swap FEs predictably after ~3 weeks offshore
Improve Junior FE competency through targeted tracking and training, enabling better level loading
Make offshore life more enjoyable by sending food, games, and entertainment to rigs
Introduce team-building activities to improve cohesion between new and existing engineers
Offset utilization reduction with increased effective utilization so cost impact is limited

categories.name: Long-term
ideas: Reinstate healthy transfer-out rates or offer short-term assignments outside Mumbai to provide variety
Recruit the right talent — set accurate expectations about the role during employer info sessions
Revisit compensation structure to remain competitive against comparable employers
Internal or on-campus marketing to promote the unique culture and rewards at SLS
Consider hiring more engineers (increases cost but reduces burnout and scheduling pressure)

recommendation: SLS's high FE attrition in Mumbai is primarily driven by a 2014 management change that created a risk-averse staffing approach: more FEs are kept idle in the office, vacations have been cut, transfer-outs have been eliminated, and Junior FEs are underutilized while Senior FEs are overloaded — eroding compensation (bonus), work-life balance, and career development simultaneously.

Immediate action should focus on making the offshore staffing model process-driven and transparent: restore predictable 3-week offshore rotations, increase vacation allocations (the math shows 14 FEs can be sent on vacation vs. 10 today), and train Junior FEs to restore management confidence in their competency.
risks: Short-term training investment for Junior FEs takes time before management confidence improves
Increasing vacation while maintaining activity coverage requires tight scheduling discipline
External pull factors (startups, graduate school) are structural and cannot be fully controlled internally
New recruits continue to dilute team culture until cohesion measures take hold
next_steps: Conduct face-to-face interviews with FEs before managers and HR to get unfiltered insight
Audit the offshore scheduling process and implement a rule-based rotation system (~3-week swaps)
Design and launch a Junior FE competency tracking and training programme
Reinstate a reasonable transfer-out quota (e.g., 3–4 per year) to restore career mobility
Benchmark FE compensation against comparable roles and present findings to CEO within 30 days
